1. The animation shows how inflation wears down the buying power of a fixed income payment. It compares a "level check", which pays the same dollar amount forever, with a "rising check", which is adjusted over time. The chart is labeled "illustrative" and uses US consumer prices (CPI-U) from Aug 2006 to Aug 2026.

2. A flat "first check" line marks the starting buying power. The grey "level check" line slides further and further below it as prices rise. The text says it is worth about 9 in 10 of its starting value by year 5. The other line, with green and yellow dots, stays much closer to the starting line. The caption "rising check: there after 20 years" appears later, and a "?" appears at the end.

3. A payment that never increases buys less every year, and the loss compounds over a long retirement. The rising check keeps its buying power much better. I'm not sure what "there after 20 years" means. My best reading is that the rising check is still roughly at its starting value after 20 years. The "?" suggests the question of which option is better is left open.

4. The animation gives no direct advice, and the footer says "history, not a forecast." A viewer might take away that inflation matters over a 20-year or longer retirement and is worth weighing when comparing the two payout options. That is only a prompt to consider it. The image doesn't say which option to choose, and it gives no starting payment amounts to compare.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the lines, the labels and the "?", and it never tells the viewer what to do.
